places.seoTitle: Netarhat: Sunrise Point, Magnolia Point, Ghaghri Falls
places.seoDescription: Netarhat, the 'Queen of Chotanagpur' at 1,128 m in Latehar: Sunrise and Magnolia points, Upper Ghaghri Falls, and Lodh Falls and Betla within reach.

overview.text: Netarhat is a hill station in Latehar district, set on one of the highest parts of the Chota Nagpur plateau at 1,128 metres and often called the 'Queen of Chotanagpur'. The plateau, about 6.4 km long and 4 km wide, is covered in thick forest of sal, kendu, mahua and eucalyptus, with pine and pear orchards planted by the Forest Department. Netarhat is best known for its views: Sunrise Point for the dawn, and Magnolia Point, 10 km away, for sunsets over the hills. Waterfalls are close by, with Upper Ghaghri Falls 4 km away and Lower Ghaghri 10 km, and the Koel river viewpoint 3 km out. Further afield are Lodh Falls, Jharkhand's highest, about 70 km away, the Mahuadanr Wolf Sanctuary and Betla National Park. Netarhat Vidyalaya, a residential school, was founded here in 1954.

places.name: Hundru Falls
places.summary: The Subarnarekha's 98-metre drop off the Ranchi plateau.
places.seoTitle: Hundru Falls near Ranchi: How to Get There, Best Season
places.seoDescription: Hundru Falls, Ranchi district: the Subarnarekha plunges 98 m off the Ranchi plateau; thunderous in the rains, a picnic spot in the dry season.

overview.text: Hundru Falls is one of the best-known sights around Ranchi. Here the Subarnarekha River drops 98 metres off the edge of the Ranchi plateau, one of the highest waterfalls in Jharkhand, and centuries of falling water have carved the rocks below into striking shapes. The falls change with the seasons: in the monsoon the river becomes a thundering torrent, while in the dry months the flow thins and the rocky basin turns into a favourite picnic spot, with a pool at the base where people bathe. The Subarnarekha hydel project lies downstream. To get there, turn off the Ranchi–Purulia road and drive about 21 km, or take the four-lane road from Ranchi through Ormanjhi and Sikidiri, about 39 km in all.

items.title: Best for

places.summary: A 43-metre hanging-valley fall below a Buddha temple, 40 km from Ranchi.
places.seoTitle: Jonha Falls (Gautamdhara) near Ranchi: 722 Steps, Getting There
places.seoDescription: Jonha (Gautamdhara) Falls, 40 km from Ranchi: a 43 m hanging-valley waterfall reached by 722 steps, with a Buddha temple on Gautam Pahar.

overview.text: Jonha Falls, also called Gautamdhara, lies about 40 km from Ranchi on the edge of the Ranchi plateau. It is a classic hanging-valley fall: the Gunga river spills over the side of the valley of its larger neighbour, the Radu, dropping 43 metres into a rocky gorge. Visitors walk down 722 steps to the base, though a road via the Jonha Fall resort lets you see the falls without the full climb. The second name, Gautamdhara, comes from the Buddha temple and ashram built on Gautam Pahar, the hill above the falls; a tourist rest house there also encloses a small Buddhist shrine. A fair is held at Jonha every Tuesday and Saturday. The falls can be reached by train, as Jonha station is only 1.5 km away, or by road off the Ranchi–Purulia highway.

places.name: Lodh Falls
places.summary: Jharkhand's highest waterfall, deep in the forests beyond Netarhat.
places.seoTitle: Lodh Falls: Jharkhand's Highest Waterfall near Netarhat
places.seoDescription: Lodh Falls, about 70 km from Netarhat: Jharkhand's highest waterfall and India's 21st highest, cascading in steps through dense sal forest.

overview.text: Lodh Falls is the highest waterfall in Jharkhand and is counted as the 21st highest in India. Fed by the clear waters of the Lodh river, it tumbles down a high rock face in a series of steps, surrounded by dense forest on the Chota Nagpur plateau, about 70 km from the hill station of Netarhat. The sound of the falls carries a long way through the trees, and reaching it is part of the experience: the approach is a walk through woodland where sunlight filters through the canopy and birdlife is rich, making the area popular with birdwatchers. Tigers, leopards and elephants roam these forests, and tribal communities with their own customs live in the region.

items.body: Highest in Jharkhand; 21st highest in India

places.seoTitle: Dimna Lake, Jamshedpur: Boating, Timings, Best Time
places.seoDescription: Dimna Lake, 13 km from Jamshedpur: a Tata Steel reservoir below the Dalma hills for boating and jet skiing; open 9 am–6 pm, best November–February.

overview.text: Dimna Lake lies 13 km from Jamshedpur, the 'Steel City', and is a man-made reservoir covering about two square miles. The dam on the Kharkai river was built under Tata Steel to end water shortages in the area, and the lake still supplies the steel plant and the city. It is also Jamshedpur's favourite outing. The water looks out on the Dalma range and is fringed with deciduous forest full of birdsong, and from November to February fog-covered hills give the mornings a magical feel. Visitors can go boating, rowing and jet skiing, take short treks into the surrounding hills, or visit the small villages around the lake for a glimpse of rural life. The drive out through rolling, green country is part of the pleasure. The lake is open from 9 am to 6 pm.

places.name: Deori Temple
places.summary: An ancient stone shrine to Kali near Tamar, preserved inside a newer temple.
places.seoTitle: Deori Temple near Ranchi: Ancient Kali Shrine
places.seoDescription: Deori Temple, about 60 km from Ranchi: an ancient shrine to a form of Kali built of interlocking stones, preserved untouched inside a newer temple.

overview.text: Deori Temple stands in the village of Deori, about 60 km from Ranchi, and is dedicated to a form of the goddess Kali. Its origins are wrapped in legend: the best-known story tells of a King of Tamar who, guided by a dream of the goddess, found the temple hidden in the forest. The old shrine is a remarkable piece of building, made of sandstone blocks that interlock without any cement or other binding material. Local belief holds that anyone who tries to alter its structure will bring down the wrath of the heavens, so the original has been left untouched; all renovation and new construction has been built around it, and the ancient shrine now sits inside a larger, newer temple. The temple draws visitors from far and wide.

images.caption: Deori Temple

places.summary: Jharkhand's highest peak and the holiest Jain pilgrimage, Shikharji.
places.seoTitle: Parasnath Hill (Shikharji): Jain Pilgrimage, Jharkhand's Highest Peak
places.seoDescription: Parasnath Hill in Giridih, 1,365 m: Shikharji, the holiest Jain pilgrimage, where Parshvanatha attained liberation; reached from Parasnath station.

overview.text: Parasnath Hill rises at the eastern end of the Chota Nagpur plateau in Giridih district and, at 1,365 metres, is the highest peak in Jharkhand. It is named after Parshvanatha, the 23rd Jain Tirthankara, who is said to have attained liberation here in the 8th century BCE, and the summit, Shikharji or Sammet Shikhar, is the holiest pilgrimage site in Jainism. On the summit stands the marble temple known as Svarna Bhadra Koot, the 'cottage of golden grace', and there is another marble Jain temple, the Jal Mandir, on the hill. The hill is also known as Marang Buru. The climb starts near Parasnath railway station.

places.summary: A long Damodar Valley dam on the Barakar with a 65 sq km lake near Dhanbad.
places.seoTitle: Maithon Dam near Dhanbad: Lake, Power Station, Getting There
places.seoDescription: Maithon Dam on the Barakar, 48 km from Dhanbad and 24 km from Asansol: a 4.8 km DVC dam with a 65 sq km lake and an underground power station.

overview.text: Maithon Dam crosses the Barakar river at Maithon, 48 km from Dhanbad and only 24 km from Asansol, which makes it one of the most visited spots in the region. The dam is about 4.8 km long and 50 metres high and holds back a lake spread over some 65 sq km, ringed by low hills. It was built by the Damodar Valley Corporation, created in 1948 as independent India's first multipurpose river valley project, designed especially for flood control, and it also generates electricity. Its underground power station is the dam's best-known feature and its main draw for visitors. The dam is also known for its natural setting and religious importance.

places.name: Massanjore Dam
places.summary: The 'Canada Dam' on the Mayurakshi in Dumka, for boating and picnics.
places.seoTitle: Massanjore Dam, Dumka: The 'Canada Dam' on the Mayurakshi
places.seoDescription: Massanjore Dam on the Mayurakshi, Dumka: a 155-foot dam built with Canadian aid and opened by Lester Pearson; boating, fishing and picnics.

overview.text: Massanjore Dam stands on the Mayurakshi river in Dumka district. It rises 155 feet from its base and impounds a reservoir covering 16,650 acres. Canadian aid helped build it, which is why it was inaugurated by Canada's foreign minister, Lester B. Pearson, and why it is also known as the Pearson Dam or Canada Dam. The dam does several jobs at once: irrigation, hydroelectric power, flood control and water supply, and by storing monsoon water and releasing it slowly it protects the land downstream and lets farmers grow crops through the year. For visitors it is a scenic spot framed by hills and forest, good for boating, fishing, walks and family picnics, with street-food stalls along the dam.

places.name: Jagannath Temple, Ranchi
places.summary: A 1691 Kalinga-style hilltop temple with Ranchi's own Rath Yatra.
places.seoTitle: Jagannath Temple, Ranchi: Hilltop Temple and Rath Yatra
places.seoDescription: Jagannath Temple, Ranchi: a 1691 hilltop temple in the Kalinga style like Puri's, rebuilt in 1992, with a Rath Yatra and fair in Aashaadha.

overview.text: Ranchi's Jagannath Temple stands on a hillock about 10 km from the city centre and can be reached either by a staircase or by road. It was built by Thakur Ani Nath Shahdeo, king of Barkagarh Jagannathpur, and completed on 25 December 1691. The temple follows the Kalinga style of Odisha and closely resembles the great Jagannath temple at Puri, though on a smaller scale. After the old structure collapsed on 6 August 1990, it was rebuilt and reopened on 8 February 1992. The temple's biggest occasion mirrors Puri's: every year in the month of Aashaadha it holds a Rath Yatra, the chariot festival, along with a large fair that draws thousands of tribal and non-tribal devotees from Ranchi and the surrounding districts.
